opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really nice example of what meta-learning can buy you when the design space is something humans have only explored with a handful of hand-crafted points. If you look at PPO, the clipping function is this fixed, static object: you clip the probability ratio at one plus or minus epsilon, and that's it, for the entire course of training. And the same goes for a lot of the preference optimization objectives like DPO. Someone sat down, derived something reasonable from first principles, and then the whole community just inherits that functional form.

But there's no reason to believe that the optimal objective is stationary over training. Early on, when your policy is close to the reference model, you might want to be quite aggressive, push hard on the preference signal. Later, when you've drifted further and the risk of overoptimization or collapse goes up, you might want to be much more conservative. And humans are just not very good at reasoning about these time-dependent dynamics. We can write down a schedule, sure, like a linear decay, but searching over the space of functions that condition on training progress is something where black-box meta-optimization really shines.

What we saw in our work on learned policy optimization, and in the follow-ups that looked at discovering preference optimization objectives, is that when you give the meta-learner access to things like the training-time fraction as an input, it discovers structure that is interpretable after the fact but that nobody would have written down a priori. For example, objectives that start out more optimistic and become more conservative, or that treat positive and negative advantages asymmetrically in ways that change over time. Then you can actually go back, distill that into a closed-form expression, and it transfers, which is the important bit. If it only worked on the exact task you meta-trained on, it would be a curiosity. The fact that these discovered objectives generalize to other environments or model scales suggests they're capturing something real about the optimization dynamics.

I'd add a caveat, though. The value is highest when your inner loop is cheap enough to evaluate many times. Doing this at frontier LLM scale is expensive, so the practical recipe is often to meta-learn on smaller proxies, using things like evolution strategies, which are very parallelizable on accelerators, and then check whether the discovered algorithm holds up when you scale. And I think that's the broader point: we should be using compute not just to train bigger models, but to search the space of learning algorithms themselves, because a lot of what we treat as fixed design choices are really just the first thing that worked.

r001.rationale: It describes starting more aggressively and becoming more conservative later in training.

r002.rationale: It says meta-optimization excels at searching the space of functions conditioned on training progress, in the context of DPO objectives.

r003.rationale: It says learned objectives can be distilled into closed-form expressions, but does not identify finding a parametric representation of the learned manifold as an unresolved problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find genuinely exciting, and it connects to a broader theme in my work, which is that a lot of the design choices in these algorithms are essentially hand-crafted priors that humans came up with because they seemed reasonable, not because anyone actually searched over the space.

So take the clipping in PPO, or the analogous regularisation in DPO, the beta term that controls how far you're allowed to drift from the reference policy. When you look at how people set these, it's a constant. Maybe they sweep it a little bit. But there's no principled reason it should be constant across training. Early on in training you might want to be quite conservative because your preference signal is noisy and you haven't figured out what's going on, and later you might want to loosen things up, or the opposite, depending on the problem. And the "right" schedule is almost certainly not something a human will guess correctly.

This is exactly where meta optimisation shines. The way we've been thinking about it, in work like Discovered Policy Optimisation and the follow-ups, is you parameterise the objective itself, including things like the clip function, as a learned function, possibly conditioned on time or training progress, and then you optimise that outer loop against some downstream performance signal. And what you find, repeatedly, is that the discovered objectives look nothing like what we would have written down by hand, but they're interpretable after the fact. You can look at them and go, oh, that actually makes sense, the algorithm is being more cautious when the advantage estimates are unreliable, and the human just never thought to do that.

Now, the caveat I'd always add is the question of generalisation. If you meta-learn a time-dependent clip schedule on one preference dataset with one model size, does it transfer? That's the real test. And my honest view is that we're in the same place that neural architecture search was ten years ago, where people were a bit sceptical and the early results were a bit overfit to the benchmark. But the trajectory is clear. Compute is getting cheaper, the outer loop is getting more tractable, and the inner loop, in this case DPO-style fine-tuning on language models, is becoming standardised enough that we can actually run these searches at meaningful scale.

The other thing I'd say is that this isn't just about squeezing out a few extra points on some alignment benchmark. The deeper value is scientific. When you meta-optimise and you look at what comes out, you learn something about the structure of the problem. If the discovered clip function has a particular shape, that's telling you something about the dynamics of preference learning that you didn't know. So I see meta optimisation as both an engineering tool and a discovery tool, and for me the discovery side is arguably the more interesting part.

r001.rationale: The candidate says early updates may be conservative, but later updates might loosen or become more conservative depending on the problem. It does not describe a shift from exploration toward increasingly conservative updates.

r002.rationale: The candidate says meta optimization can search over hand-designed choices by learning the clip function conditioned on time or training progress, and calls this where meta optimization shines.

r003.rationale: The candidate proposes parameterizing and learning the time-dependent clip function, but does not identify finding a parametric representation of its manifold as an unresolved problem in Foerster’s work.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal is that you don’t have to assume that the same clipping rule is appropriate throughout training. Early on, you might want quite different update behaviour from what you want when the policy is close to convergence. Meta-optimization gives you a way to learn that schedule against an outer objective, rather than choosing it entirely by hand.

The important question is whether what you learn transfers. Does the clip function work across different tasks, initializations, and training horizons, or has it just fitted the particular training setup you used to discover it? I’d want to compare it with fairly simple schedules and see whether the extra complexity actually buys you something.

So I see it as useful both for designing an optimizer and for discovering principles. If you can inspect the learned function and understand why its behaviour changes over time, you might be able to turn that into a simpler, more general rule.

r001.rationale: It contrasts early training with near convergence, but does not specify a shift from exploration toward more conservative updates.

r002.rationale: It says meta-optimization can learn a time-varying schedule, but does not explain its particular suitability for the large design space created by allowing clip functions to vary over training.

r003.rationale: It discusses inspecting and simplifying a learned function, but does not identify finding a parametric representation of the clip-function manifold as an unresolved problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an interesting direction, because there’s no obvious reason that the same clipping rule should be optimal throughout training. Early on, you might want to allow larger changes, whereas later you might want a more conservative update. Meta optimization gives you a way of learning that schedule rather than choosing it by hand.

But the crucial question is: what are you optimizing the schedule for? If the outer objective is just performance on the same preference data, you may discover something that exploits that particular dataset without improving the policy in a broader sense. You’d want held-out evaluation, and you’d want to compare against a simple schedule with the same tuning budget.

So I’d see the value both in potentially improving training and in understanding what a good clipping rule looks like. If the learned rule turns out to be simple, that’s particularly useful: you can extract a design principle rather than having to run an expensive meta-optimization procedure every time.

r001.rationale: It says larger changes may be useful early in training and more conservative updates later, communicating the progression from exploration-like updates toward conservatism.

r002.rationale: It says meta optimization can learn a schedule, but does not explain why it is particularly suited to the large design space of clip functions varying with optimization progress.

r003.rationale: It does not identify finding a parametric representation of the learned time-dependent clip-function manifold as an unresolved problem.
